targetSkill: Teach the student to identify the mood a writer creates in the reader — separate from what characters feel — by reading diction, imagery, omission, and rhythm as deliberate authorial choices.
mustHave: A single dominant mood that is nameable in one word (tense, melancholy, ominous, hopeful, grief-struck, peaceful, dread-filled, wistful, suspenseful, eerie, oppressive, serene — choose one)
Mood built through at least two of: diction (word choice), imagery (sensory detail), omission (what is conspicuously unsaid), rhythm (sentence length and pacing)
Observable mood signals — specific words or phrases a reader can point to as the source of the feeling
Mood that lives in the writing itself, not in character dialogue stating an emotion
mustNotHave: Multiple competing moods (shifts from fear to joy mid-paragraph)
Mood that depends on a character stating their emotion directly (e.g., 'She was sad'). Mood must live in the prose, not in what characters say they feel.
Mood that requires knowledge of surrounding story context to land — paragraph must stand alone
Paragraphs dominated by dialogue (60%+ quotation marks)
Mood created primarily through exclamation points or melodrama rather than craft
Archaic or heavily poetic prose that obscures mood signals behind unfamiliar syntax

tierSignals.tier1: Mood is thick and unmistakable. Signals concrete and repeated (rain, darkness, silence, cold). A student notices the feeling on first read.
tierSignals.tier2: Mood is present but subtler. Requires noticing 3 or more contributing signals working together. Student must slow down to feel it.
tierSignals.tier3: Mood is built more through omission or rhythm than through diction. Requires sharper attention. Student must re-read to identify what's doing the work.
